summary:
Zbadaj Swoje Pole (“Check Your Field”) helps Polish farmers prove that drought hit their own field. A farmer clicks their parcel on a map, picks the crop, and gets a free verdict on whether the season showed signs of drought stress. If they need it on paper, they can download a PDF report to show their insurer.

details:
Zbadaj Swoje Pole (“Check Your Field”)

When a drought hits a Polish farm, nobody comes out to look at the field. Hail or frost gets a local commission, but drought is decided by a model that gives one yes-or-no answer for the whole municipality. If your field dried out and the model says your area was fine, you have nothing to show anyone. The scale of the problem is real: in the dry years 2018–2019 Polish farmers lost about PLN 8.8 billion a year to drought, while got paid out around PLN 2.3 billion a year for drought damage (Supreme Audit Office, NIK).

Our app gives the farmer a document about their own field. You find your parcel on the map, click it, and pick what you grow. Within a minute you get a free verdict: no signal, moderate or strong evidence that your crop went through drought stress. If you need it on paper, you buy a PDF report that you can hand to your insurer. We see it a bit like a vehicle history report, only for a field.

The report puts four things side by side. First, the statutory drought test from Polish law, using the official water-balance thresholds for that crop and soil. Then what the plants actually did, from satellite vegetation indices over the whole season compared with what that crop normally looks like in the area. Then soil moisture. And finally, whether the dry spell landed in the crop’s critical growth stage, because a dry June ruins wheat while a dry August barely touches it.

Everything comes from free, public data: NASA HLS and SMAP, Copernicus Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2, the national agricultural drought monitoring system (IUNG-PIB) and the official land registry service (GUGiK). That was a deliberate choice. The farmer and the insurer can both check the same numbers, so the argument is about the field, not about whose data to trust. NISAR is our next step. Its L-band radar sees soil moisture through clouds, and cloudy weeks are exactly when optical satellites go blind.

A few decisions shaped the project. We sell only to farmers, so there’s no conflict of interest with insurers. The price depends on hectares, not on the result, so we never get paid more for finding drought. The report documents growing conditions and doesn’t promise compensation. We compare each field with the typical curve for its declared crop rather than with its own history, because crop rotation would make that comparison meaningless.

For the hackathon we designed the user flow, built an animated walkthrough of the app in HTML/CSS rendered with Python, and wrote a full sample report for a demonstration parcel in Kujawy, set against the real 2026 drought season. We used AI tools to help with research, drafting and the walkthrough, and checked every figure against its primary source.
